questions.question: What are argument matchers in Mockito and how do you use them?
questions.title: Mockito Argument Matchers | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Argument matchers in Mockito let you stub and verify method calls with flexible patterns instead of exact values. any() matches any argument, eq(value) matches a specific value, and type-specific matchers like anyString() or anyInt() match by type. When using matchers, all arguments in that method call must be matchers—if you need to mix a matcher with a literal, wrap the literal with eq().

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Mockito's flexible stubbing and verification patterns beyond hardcoded values
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing matcher and exact value arguments like when(mock.method(any(), 'literal')) which throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the all-or-none rule clearly: if any argument uses a matcher, all must use matchers, wrapping literals with eq() when needed

sections.title: What Argument Matchers Are and Why They Matter
sections.content: **Argument matchers** are Mockito utilities that let you define flexible matching rules for method arguments instead of requiring exact values. When writing unit tests, you often don't care about the exact value passed to a dependency—you care about the pattern or type. For example, you might want to stub a repository method to return a specific user whenever *any* valid email is passed, not just one hardcoded email. Think of matchers as wildcards in stubbing and verification: **any()** is like a wildcard that accepts anything, **anyString()** accepts any String, and **eq(value)** matches exactly one value. Matchers make tests less brittle because they focus on behavior rather than exact data. The core concept: Mockito records matcher calls in thread-local state, which is why you must use matchers for all arguments or none—mixing breaks this state machine.

sections.title: Using Argument Matchers in Stubbing and Verification
Key Points
content: **any()**: matches any argument including null in Mockito 3+; use for arguments you don't care about in the test
**anyString(), anyInt(), anyLong()**: type-specific matchers that match any value of that primitive or wrapper type
**eq(value)**: wraps a literal value as a matcher; required when mixing matchers and exact values in the same call
**All-or-none rule**: if any argument in a method call uses a matcher, all arguments must use matchers—mixing causes InvalidUseOfMatchersException
**Verification with matchers**: verify(mock).method(anyString()) asserts the method was called with any String, not a specific one
**Matchers in stubbing**: when(mock.method(any())).thenReturn(x) stubs the method for any argument value, making tests more flexible
**Common types**: any(ClassName.class) matches any instance of that class; isNull() and isNotNull() match null or non-null explicitly

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Argument matchers in Mockito let you stub and verify method calls without hardcoding exact argument values. Instead of saying this mock returns X only when you pass this exact string, you can say it returns X when you pass any string at all. The most common matcher is any, which matches anything. You also have type-specific ones like anyString or anyInt, and eq for exact values. Here's the key rule that trips people up: if you use a matcher for one argument, you must use matchers for all arguments in that method call. So if you write when parenthesis mock dot method parenthesis anyString comma 42 parenthesis, Mockito throws an error because you mixed a matcher with a raw number. You'd fix it by wrapping 42 with eq like eq parenthesis 42 parenthesis. That's because Mockito records matchers in thread-local state and mixing breaks that mechanism. In verification, matchers work the same way: verify parenthesis mock parenthesis dot method parenthesis anyString parenthesis asserts the method was called with some string, without caring what it was. One pitfall is overusing any when you should verify the actual value—if the argument matters for correctness, don't wildcard it. Use matchers to make tests flexible where flexibility makes sense, but not to hide bugs by ignoring important data. The balance is: match on patterns when the exact value doesn't affect the test outcome, but assert specific values when they do.

questions.question: How do you use argThat() for custom argument matching in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito argThat Custom Matcher | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: argThat accepts a custom predicate to match arguments based on domain logic. You pass a lambda or method reference that returns true if the argument meets your criteria. Use it when built-in matchers aren't expressive enough—for example, matching an Order only if its total exceeds 100 and status is PENDING.

sections.title: Custom Matching with argThat for Complex Conditions
sections.content: **argThat(predicate)** is Mockito's escape hatch for custom argument matching. Built-in matchers like anyString or any work for simple cases, but real-world tests often need domain-specific logic: "match this Order if it's over 100 dollars and marked PENDING" or "match this Request if it has exactly three items and a valid timestamp." Think of argThat as a filter: you give it a lambda or method reference that takes the argument and returns true or false. If true, Mockito considers it a match. This is powerful because it keeps your test assertions precise without requiring exact object equality. For example, instead of mocking a method to return X for one hardcoded Order object, you can return X for *any* Order that meets your business rule. The predicate you pass is a **Predicate<T>** or **ArgumentMatcher<T>**, and Mockito evaluates it during stubbing or verification. One key detail: your predicate must handle null arguments safely, or wrap it in a null check, because Mockito may pass null if the method is called with null.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: argThat lets you write custom matching logic for method arguments when the built-in matchers aren't enough. You pass it a predicate—a lambda or method reference—that takes the argument and returns true if it matches your rule. For example, say you're testing an OrderService and you want to verify that it saves orders only if the total is over a hundred dollars and the status is PENDING. You can't express that with any or eq, so you use argThat with a lambda: argThat parenthesis order arrow order dot getTotal greater-than 100 and order dot getStatus equals Status dot PENDING parenthesis. Mockito evaluates that lambda every time the method is called, and if it returns true, the argument matches. You can use argThat in both stubbing and verification. In stubbing, it lets you return different values based on argument properties. In verification, it asserts that the method was called with an argument meeting your criteria. One thing to watch out for: your predicate must handle null arguments safely, because Mockito might pass null if the method is called with null. So you'd write order not-equals null and order dot getTotal greater-than 100. For readability, extract the lambda to a named method if the logic is complex or reused—something like argThat parenthesis this colon-colon isHighValuePending parenthesis. That makes the test intent clearer. The key advantage over eq is that you're not relying on the equals method being implemented correctly on the object, which is often missing in POJOs or entities.

questions.direct_answer: Argument matchers work identically in verify as they do in when—use them to assert that a method was called with arguments matching a pattern rather than exact values. This is essential when the exact argument isn't predictable or when you only care about specific properties of a complex object.

sections.title: Argument Matchers in Verification for Flexible Assertions
sections.content: **Mockito's verify method** checks that a mock was called with specific arguments, and you can use **argument matchers** in verify just like you do in when. Instead of verifying exact values—verify(mock).method("alice@example.com")—you can verify patterns—verify(mock).method(anyString()). This is useful when the exact argument isn't known at test-writing time or when you only care about part of the argument's state. For example, in a test where a service generates a random transaction ID and passes it to a repository, you can't predict the exact ID, so you verify with anyString(). Or if you're verifying that a method was called with a User object, but you only care that the user's role is ADMIN, you'd use argThat(user -> user.getRole() == Role.ADMIN). Think of verify with matchers as asserting *that something happened matching this pattern*, not *that something happened with this exact data*. The key principle: **verify should be as specific as the test requires**—use any only when the argument truly doesn't matter for the behavior you're testing, otherwise you risk false positives where the test passes but the wrong value was used.

sections.title: Using Matchers in verify for Flexible Assertion

content: **Matchers in verify**: use the same matchers (any, anyString, argThat) in verify as in when to assert method calls with flexible argument patterns
**When to use any**: only when the argument value truly doesn't affect the test outcome—overusing any hides bugs where wrong data is passed
**When to use specific matchers**: when the argument is critical to the behavior being tested, assert the exact value or use a targeted matcher like eq or argThat

**Mixing matchers and exact values**: remember the all-or-none rule—verify parenthesis mock parenthesis dot method parenthesis eq parenthesis value parenthesis comma anyString parenthesis is correct, but verify parenthesis mock parenthesis dot method parenthesis value comma anyString parenthesis throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException

**argThat in verify**: powerful for complex assertions—verify parenthesis repo parenthesis dot save parenthesis argThat parenthesis order arrow order dot getTotal greater-than 100 parenthesis asserts the saved order met your domain rule
**Readability trade-off**: using any makes tests less brittle but also less precise; if a test starts failing, specific matchers give better diagnostics than any
**verifyNoMoreInteractions**: after verify with matchers, use this to ensure no unexpected calls happened, catching side effects you didn't intend

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Argument matchers work the same way in verify as they do in when—you use them to assert that a method was called with arguments matching a pattern instead of exact values. For example, if you're testing a NotificationService and you want to verify it sent an email to a user but you don't care about the exact message text, you'd write verify parenthesis emailSender parenthesis dot send parenthesis anyString parenthesis. That asserts the method was called with some string, without specifying what it was. This is really useful when the exact argument isn't predictable—like a generated ID or timestamp—or when you only care about part of the argument. Say you're verifying that a repository saved an Order, but you only care that the order total was over a hundred dollars. You'd use verify parenthesis repo parenthesis dot save parenthesis argThat parenthesis order arrow order dot getTotal greater-than 100 parenthesis. That's more flexible than requiring an exact Order instance. The key balance is knowing when to use any versus a specific matcher. If the argument matters for correctness—like the user ID or transaction amount—don't use any, because that hides bugs. Use any only when the value genuinely doesn't affect the test outcome. For example, verifying that a logger was called with any message is fine because the message format usually doesn't affect business logic. One pitfall is overusing any everywhere—that makes tests pass even when wrong data is passed, giving you false confidence. The rule of thumb: be as specific as the test requires. If you need domain-specific checks, use argThat. If the exact value matters, use eq. If it truly doesn't matter, use any.

questions.question: What is the difference between any() and any(ClassName.class) in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito any() vs any(Class) | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: any matches any non-null argument regardless of type, while any parenthesis ClassName dot class parenthesis matches any non-null argument of that specific type. In Mockito 2 and later, any does not match null by default—use isNull, nullable parenthesis ClassName dot class parenthesis, or any explicitly combined with null checks for null handling.

sections.title: Type-Specific Matchers and Null Handling in Mockito
sections.content: **any()** and **any(ClassName.class)** both match arguments, but with subtle differences in type safety and null handling. any() is a wildcard matcher that accepts any argument of any type, as long as it's non-null in Mockito 2+. any(ClassName.class) is type-specific: it matches any non-null instance of ClassName or its subtypes. The key distinction is **null handling**. In Mockito 1, any() matched null arguments, which caused confusion and bugs. In Mockito 2 onward, any() and any(ClassName.class) **do not match null by default**. To explicitly match null, use **isNull()** or **nullable(ClassName.class)**. This change makes tests more explicit about null expectations. Think of any(ClassName.class) as a type-safe version of any: it enforces that the argument is the right type at compile time and rejects null at runtime. Use any() when the type doesn't matter and you're sure the argument won't be null. Use any(ClassName.class) when you want type safety and clarity. Use nullable(ClassName.class) or isNull() when null is a valid argument in your test scenario.

sections.title: any() vs any(ClassName.class) vs Null Matchers
When to Use Each Matcher
sections.content: **Use any()** when the argument type is irrelevant to the test and you know it will never be null—for example, verifying that a logger was called with some message, regardless of content or type. **Use any(ClassName.class)** when you want type safety and the argument must be a specific type but you don't care about its value—for example, stubbing a repository to return a default user for any UserId instance. This prevents accidental calls with the wrong type. **Use nullable(ClassName.class)** when the method can receive either a valid instance or null, and you want to stub or verify both cases—for example, a findById method that returns null for missing records. **Use isNull()** when you specifically want to match null arguments in verification—for example, asserting that a cleanup method was called with null to reset state. The Mockito 2 change means you must be explicit about null: if you write any() expecting it to match null, your test will fail. Always check the Mockito version in your project and use nullable or isNull when null is part of the method contract.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **any()**: matches any non-null argument of any type; does not match null in Mockito 2 and later
**any(ClassName.class)**: type-safe matcher that matches any non-null instance of ClassName or its subtypes; enforces type at compile time
**Mockito 1 vs 2 change**: Mockito 1's any matched null, Mockito 2 plus any does not—this prevents accidental null matches and makes tests more explicit
**nullable(ClassName.class)**: matches any instance of ClassName or null; use when null is a valid argument in the method contract
**isNull()**: matches only null arguments; use in verify to assert that null was passed explicitly
**isNotNull()**: matches any non-null argument, equivalent to any but more semantically clear when null-handling is the focus
**Type safety**: any parenthesis Order dot class parenthesis gives compile-time type checking, preventing mismatches between stubbing and actual method signature

The key difference is type safety and null handling. If you write any, it accepts anything—a String, an Integer, a custom Order object—as long as it's not null. If you write any parenthesis Order dot class parenthesis, it only accepts Order instances or subtypes, and still doesn't match null. The reason you'd use the typed version is for compile-time safety. So if you're stubbing a method that can receive null, use nullable. If you're verifying that null was passed, use isNull. The practical takeaway is: check your Mockito version. questions.title: ArgumentCaptor in Mockito

sections.title: Capturing and Asserting on Mock Method Arguments
sections.content: **ArgumentCaptor<T>** is a Mockito utility that captures the actual argument passed to a mock method so you can inspect and assert on it after the call. Unlike matchers like any() or argThat(), which match during the call, a captor *records* the argument and gives it back to you for detailed verification. This is essential when you're testing that a service passes the correct data to a dependency, but the data is a complex object with multiple fields. For example, if your OrderService calls repository.save(order), you want to verify not just that save was called, but that the order had the right customer ID, status, and timestamp. Think of ArgumentCaptor as a recording device: you tell Mockito "capture whatever was passed to this method," then you retrieve it with getValue() and write assertions. You create a captor with **ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class)** or use the **@Captor** annotation for cleaner code. In verify, you pass **captor.capture()** where the argument goes, and Mockito records the actual value. If the method is called multiple times, use **captor.getAllValues()** to get a list of all captured arguments.

sections.title: Using ArgumentCaptor to Assert on Captured Arguments
Key Points
content: **ArgumentCaptor<T>**: captures the argument passed to a mock method so you can retrieve it later and perform detailed assertions on its state
**Creating a captor**: use ArgumentCaptor dot forClass parenthesis ClassName dot class parenthesis or annotate a field with at-Captor for cleaner test setup
**Capturing in verify**: call verify parenthesis mock parenthesis dot method parenthesis captor dot capture parenthesis to record the argument during verification
**Retrieving the value**: use captor dot getValue to get the captured argument after verify; throws exception if the method wasn't called or was called multiple times without getAllValues
**Multiple calls**: if the method was called N times, use captor dot getAllValues to get a List of all captured arguments, then assert on each or filter
**When to use**: when you need to assert on properties of a complex object passed to a dependency, and matchers like argThat aren't expressive enough or hurt readability
**Alternative to thenAnswer**: instead of inspecting arguments inside a thenAnswer callback, use a captor for clearer separation of stubbing and assertion logic

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ArgumentCaptor captures the actual argument passed to a mock method so you can inspect it after the call and perform detailed assertions on its state. This is super useful when you're testing that a service passes the right data to a dependency, but the data is a complex object with multiple fields. For example, say you have an OrderService that calls repository dot save with an Order object. You want to verify not just that save was called, but that the Order had the correct customer ID, status, and items. You create a captor with ArgumentCaptor dot forClass parenthesis Order dot class parenthesis, or use the at-Captor annotation on a field which is cleaner. Then in your test, you call verify parenthesis repo parenthesis dot save parenthesis captor dot capture parenthesis. That tells Mockito to record whatever Order was passed. After verify, you call captor dot getValue to retrieve the captured Order, then you write assertions on it—assertThat capturedOrder dot getCustomerId equals 123, assertThat capturedOrder dot getStatus equals PENDING, and so on. If the method was called multiple times, you use captor dot getAllValues which returns a List of all captured arguments. Then you can assert on each one or filter the list. The key advantage over using argThat is readability: instead of cramming all your assertions into a lambda inside verify, you capture the argument and write normal assertions afterward. That makes the test easier to read and debug. One pitfall is calling getValue when the method was called multiple times—it throws an exception. Always check if you expect multiple calls and use getAllValues instead. The at-Captor annotation is preferred over ArgumentCaptor dot forClass because it's less boilerplate and integrates with MockitoExtension to initialize the captor automatically.

questions.title: Mixing ArgumentMatchers with Real Values
questions.direct_answer: You cannot mix argument matchers and real values in the same method call—Mockito requires either all arguments to be matchers or all to be real values. If you need to mix, wrap the real value with eq parenthesis value parenthesis to turn it into a matcher. This is because matchers use thread-local state, and mixing raw values bypasses that mechanism, causing InvalidUseOfMatchersException.

sections.title: The All-or-None Rule for Argument Matchers
sections.content: **Mockito's cardinal rule for argument matchers**: if you use a matcher for *any* argument in a method call, you must use matchers for *all* arguments. You cannot mix matchers like any() with raw literal values like 42 or "hello". For example, when(mock.method(anyString(), 42)) throws **InvalidUseOfMatchersException**. The fix is to wrap the literal with **eq(42)**: when(mock.method(anyString(), eq(42))). This rule exists because Mockito records matchers in a **thread-local stack**. When you call anyString(), Mockito pushes a matcher onto the stack. When you pass a raw value like 42, Mockito doesn't push anything. Later, when Mockito tries to match the actual method call, it expects the stack to have exactly as many matchers as there are arguments. A mismatch causes the exception. Think of it like filling out a form: you can either fill out all fields with wildcards or all with exact values, but you can't mix—the system can't process half-wildcard, half-exact input. In practice, this means wrapping every literal with eq() whenever you use at least one matcher in that call.

sections.title: Correct and Incorrect Matcher Mixing
Key Points
content: **All-or-none rule**: if any argument in a method call uses a matcher, all arguments must use matchers—mixing throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException
**eq(value)**: wraps a literal value as a matcher; use it to turn raw values into matchers when mixing is required
**Thread-local stack**: Mockito records matchers in thread-local state; each matcher call pushes to the stack, raw values don't, causing stack misalignment if mixed
**Applies to stubbing and verification**: the rule applies to both when parenthesis mock dot method parenthesis and verify parenthesis mock parenthesis dot method parenthesis

**Common mistake**: writing when parenthesis mock dot method parenthesis anyString comma 42 parenthesis instead of when parenthesis mock dot method parenthesis anyString comma eq parenthesis 42 parenthesis parenthesis
**Why the rule exists**: Mockito can't distinguish between "you want to match any value" and "you want to match this exact value" if matchers and raw values are mixed, so it enforces consistency
**Exception message**: InvalidUseOfMatchersException says "matchers can't be mixed with actual values"—always check the argument list when you see this

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The rule is simple but easy to forget: you cannot mix argument matchers and real values in the same method call. Either all arguments use matchers or all use real values. If you try to mix them, Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException. For example, if you write when parenthesis mock dot charge parenthesis anyString comma 100 parenthesis dot thenReturn parenthesis true parenthesis, you'll get an error because anyString is a matcher but 100 is a raw value. The fix is to wrap 100 with eq: when parenthesis mock dot charge parenthesis anyString comma eq parenthesis 100 parenthesis parenthesis dot thenReturn parenthesis true parenthesis. Now both arguments are matchers and Mockito is happy. The reason for this rule is how Mockito works internally. When you call a matcher like anyString, Mockito records it in a thread-local stack. When you pass a raw value like 100, nothing gets recorded. Later, when Mockito tries to match the actual method invocation, it expects the number of recorded matchers to equal the number of arguments. If they don't match, it throws an exception because it can't figure out which argument should match what. Think of it like a form: you either fill out all fields with wildcards or all with exact answers, but you can't mix. This rule applies to both stubbing with when and verification with verify. A common mistake freshers make is writing verify parenthesis mock parenthesis dot method parenthesis any comma literal parenthesis and not understanding why it fails. The fix is always the same: wrap the literal with eq. So verify parenthesis mock parenthesis dot method parenthesis any comma eq parenthesis literal parenthesis parenthesis. The practical takeaway: if you use even one matcher, wrap all your literals with eq. It's a bit verbose but it keeps Mockito's internal state consistent.

sections.title: The eq Matcher and Why It Exists
sections.content: **eq(value)** is an argument matcher that matches a specific exact value—it's the matcher equivalent of passing a raw literal. At first glance, this seems redundant: why write eq(42) when you can just write 42? The reason is **Mockito's all-or-none rule**: if you use a matcher for any argument in a method call, you must use matchers for all arguments. eq() lets you turn a literal value into a matcher so you can mix it with other matchers. For example, when(mock.process(anyString(), 100)) throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException because anyString() is a matcher but 100 is a raw value. The fix is when(mock.process(anyString(), eq(100)))—now both arguments are matchers. Internally, eq(value) is a pass-through: it simply checks that the actual argument equals the given value using .equals(). Think of eq() as a bridge between Mockito's matcher system and your literal values. You wouldn't use it if all your arguments are raw values—when(mock.process("id", 100)) is fine. You only need eq() when mixing matchers with literals in the same call.

sections.title: Using eq to Mix Matchers with Literal Values

content: **eq(value)**: wraps a literal value as an argument matcher; matches if the actual argument equals the given value using dot equals
**When to use**: only when mixing matchers with literals in the same method call—if all arguments are literals, eq is unnecessary
**All-or-none rule**: Mockito requires all arguments to be matchers or all to be raw values; eq turns a literal into a matcher to satisfy this rule
**Pass-through behavior**: eq parenthesis 42 parenthesis is functionally equivalent to passing 42 directly, but it satisfies Mockito's matcher stack requirement
**Common pattern**: when parenthesis mock dot method parenthesis anyString comma eq parenthesis literal parenthesis parenthesis is the correct way to mix a wildcard matcher with a specific value

sections.content: eq wraps a literal value as an argument matcher so you can mix it with other matchers in the same method call. The reason you need it is Mockito's all-or-none rule: if you use a matcher for any argument, you must use matchers for all arguments. For example, say you're stubbing a method that takes a user ID and a status. You want to match any user ID but only the ACTIVE status. If you write when parenthesis repo dot updateStatus parenthesis anyLong comma UserStatus dot ACTIVE parenthesis, Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException because anyLong is a matcher but UserStatus dot ACTIVE is a raw value. The fix is to wrap the status with eq: when parenthesis repo dot updateStatus parenthesis anyLong comma eq parenthesis UserStatus dot ACTIVE parenthesis parenthesis. Now both arguments are matchers and Mockito is happy. Internally, eq is just a pass-through—it checks that the actual argument equals the value you passed using dot equals. So eq parenthesis 42 parenthesis matches the argument 42, and eq parenthesis status parenthesis matches that exact status. You wouldn't use eq if all your arguments are raw values—when parenthesis mock dot method parenthesis literal1 comma literal2 parenthesis is fine because no matchers are involved. You only need eq when you're mixing. The same applies to verify. If you write verify parenthesis repo parenthesis dot updateStatus parenthesis anyLong comma UserStatus dot ACTIVE parenthesis, it fails. You have to write verify parenthesis repo parenthesis dot updateStatus parenthesis anyLong comma eq parenthesis UserStatus dot ACTIVE parenthesis. The practical takeaway is: whenever you use a matcher like any or anyString, wrap all your literal values with eq in that same call. It's a bit verbose but it keeps Mockito's internal state consistent.

sections.title: Custom Argument Matchers for Complex Domain Logic
sections.content: **ArgumentMatcher<T>** is a Mockito interface you implement to create custom matching logic when built-in matchers and lambdas aren't expressive or reusable enough. You implement the **matches(T argument)** method, which returns true if the argument satisfies your criteria. You then pass an instance of your matcher to **argThat()** in stubbing or verification. This is useful for complex domain rules that you want to reuse across multiple tests: for example, "match an Order if it's high-value, shipped to a priority region, and placed within the last 24 hours." While you can write such logic as a lambda—argThat(order -> order.getTotal() > 1000 && ...)—a named ArgumentMatcher class is clearer and easier to test. Think of ArgumentMatcher as a named predicate with explicit intent. The matches method receives the actual argument from the method call, and you return true or false. **Null safety** is critical: if the method can receive null, your matches implementation must check for null explicitly, or Mockito will pass null to your code and you'll get a NullPointerException. Java 8 plus lambda syntax makes this simpler for one-off cases, but a class is better for complex or reused logic.

sections.title: Custom ArgumentMatcher with Class and Lambda
Key Points
content: **ArgumentMatcher<T>**: interface with one method matches parenthesis T argument parenthesis that returns boolean; implement it for custom matching logic
**Class-based matcher**: create a class implementing ArgumentMatcher for reusable, named, testable matching logic—better for complex domain rules
**Lambda form**: use argThat parenthesis lambda parenthesis for one-off custom matching—simpler but less reusable than a named class
**Null safety**: your matches implementation must handle null arguments explicitly—Mockito passes null if the method receives null, causing NullPointerException if unchecked
**When to use**: when built-in matchers like any or eq aren't expressive enough and the logic is complex or domain-specific
**Reusability**: a named ArgumentMatcher class can be used across multiple tests and even unit-tested itself for correctness
**Combining matchers**: you can use multiple argThat calls in the same method if each argument needs custom logic—remember the all-or-none rule applies

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To write a custom argument matcher, you implement the ArgumentMatcher interface with a matches method that takes the argument and returns true if it matches your criteria. Then you pass an instance of your matcher to argThat in stubbing or verification. For example, say you want to verify that a repository saves only high-value orders—orders with a total over 500 and status PENDING. You create a class called HighValueOrderMatcher that implements ArgumentMatcher of Order. In the matches method, you check if the order is not null, the total is over 500, and the status is PENDING. Then you return true if all conditions are met. In your test, you call verify parenthesis repo parenthesis dot save parenthesis argThat parenthesis new HighValueOrderMatcher parenthesis. That asserts the saved order met your criteria. The advantage of a class-based matcher over a lambda is reusability and readability—you can use the same matcher in multiple tests and the class name makes the intent clear. If you only need the matcher once, you can use a lambda directly in argThat: argThat parenthesis order arrow order not-equals null and order dot getTotal greater-than 500 parenthesis. That's simpler for one-off cases. The key pitfall is null safety. If the method can receive null and you don't check for it in your matches method, you'll get a NullPointerException. Always write order not-equals null as the first condition. In Java 8 plus, lambdas are the most common form, but if your matching logic is complex or shared across tests, a named class is cleaner. You can even unit-test the matcher itself to ensure it works correctly before using it in integration tests. The practical rule: use a lambda for simple one-off checks, use a class for complex or reused logic.
